title: Skin Cancer Recognition: Risk, Change, and the Lesion That Does Not Heal
bottomLine: Skin-cancer assessment is risk- and lesion-driven. A changing pigmented lesion, nonhealing/bleeding lesion, rapidly growing keratotic lesion or suspicious lesion in an immunocompromised patient requires diagnostic evaluation rather than reassurance or population-screening language.
recognize: Melanoma warning signs include asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter/evolution and an 'ugly duckling' lesion that differs from the patient's other nevi.
BCC often presents as a pearly/translucent papule, scar-like plaque or recurrently bleeding nonhealing lesion; SCC may be keratotic, crusted, tender, ulcerated or rapidly enlarging.
differentiate: Actinic keratosis is premalignant field damage rather than invasive cancer, but induration, tenderness, rapid growth or ulceration raises SCC concern.
Seborrheic keratoses and benign nevi can mimic malignancy; evolution and dermoscopic/biopsy assessment resolve uncertainty.
assessment: Assess personal/family skin-cancer history, UV/tanning exposure, immunosuppression/transplant, lesion duration/evolution, bleeding, pain and prior treatment.
Examine the lesion plus regional skin/lymph nodes when malignancy is suspected and include palms, soles and nails when clinically relevant.
workup: A suspicious lesion needs an appropriate biopsy technique that preserves diagnostic architecture/depth; dermoscopy can refine assessment but does not replace histopathology when melanoma or invasive carcinoma is plausible.
management: Arrange timely biopsy or dermatology/surgical referral based on malignancy suspicion and site; do not repeatedly destroy or treat an undiagnosed suspicious lesion empirically.
After a confirmed cancer, treatment and surveillance are tumour/site/risk specific.
medicationSafety: Do not use prolonged topical steroid/anti-inflammatory therapy to suppress a persistent evolving lesion without diagnostic reassessment.
redFlags: New firm nodule on sun-exposed skin
Pigmented nail lesion with concerning evolution
counselling: Teach self-examination for new/changing lesions and sun protection without implying skin cancer occurs only in fair skin; melanoma and other cancers occur in all skin tones.
followUp: Own pathology results and ensure definitive treatment/referral; patients with prior skin cancer need risk-based surveillance.
examTrap: Calling a symptomatic changing lesion 'screening' and scheduling routine follow-up instead of moving to diagnostic biopsy/referral.
oneLinePearl: Screening is for asymptomatic risk; a changing lesion is already a diagnostic problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association skin cancer resources

title: Melanoma: Evolution and Depth Matter More Than Reassuring Colour
bottomLine: Suspected melanoma requires prompt complete diagnostic assessment and an appropriately planned biopsy because tumour depth drives staging and treatment. Do not reassure from small size, symmetry alone, or the absence of dark pigment—amelanotic and acral melanomas occur.
recognize: ABCDE/evolution and ugly-duckling change are high-yield clues; nodular melanoma can grow quickly and may be raised rather than classically asymmetric.
Acral melanoma can occur on palms, soles and nail units and is especially important in darker skin tones.
differentiate: Benign nevi, seborrheic keratoses, subungual hematoma and pigmented BCC can mimic melanoma; history of evolution and dermoscopic/biopsy findings decide.
assessment: Document evolution, symptoms, lesion dimensions/location, personal/family melanoma history, immunosuppression and regional nodes when concerning.
workup: Use complete/excisional biopsy with narrow margins when feasible for a suspicious melanoma so Breslow depth can be measured; avoid superficial sampling that could compromise staging when a full-thickness diagnostic biopsy is practical.
management: Refer confirmed/suspected melanoma for definitive excision and stage-appropriate oncology/surgical management; sentinel-node decisions depend on tumour features and are specialist-led.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly freeze, shave superficially or apply empiric topical therapy to a lesion that could be melanoma.
redFlags: Rapidly changing pigmented or amelanotic lesion
New lesion in a melanoma survivor
counselling: Teach that melanoma may be brown, black, red, pink or relatively nonpigmented and can arise in non-sun-exposed/acral sites.
followUp: Track pathology through definitive treatment and ensure risk-based skin/nodal surveillance.
examTrap: Using a superficial shave that transects a strongly suspected melanoma and obscures accurate depth when a full-thickness diagnostic approach is feasible.
oneLinePearl: For melanoma, evolution finds it and depth stages it.

title: Basal Cell Carcinoma: Low Metastatic Risk Does Not Mean No Treatment
bottomLine: BCC rarely metastasizes but can progressively destroy local tissue. Confirm the diagnosis and choose treatment from tumour subtype, size, borders, location, recurrence status and patient factors; high-risk facial or recurrent tumours often need margin-controlled specialist surgery.
recognize: Pearly/translucent papule with telangiectasia, recurrently bleeding sore, red scaly patch or scar-like plaque are common BCC patterns.
differentiate: SCC is often more keratotic/indurated and carries greater metastatic risk; melanoma and benign lesions can mimic pigmented BCC.
assessment: Assess size, location, border definition, recurrence, immunosuppression, prior radiation and symptoms such as pain/neurologic change suggesting deeper invasion.
workup: Biopsy establishes histologic subtype before definitive management when diagnosis/risk is uncertain.
management: Low-risk lesions may be treated with standard excision or selected destructive/topical modalities; high-risk/recurrent lesions and functionally sensitive sites warrant dermatologic surgery/Mohs or other specialist treatment.
medicationSafety: Do not use topical therapy for a lesion whose subtype/depth/location makes surgery the safer definitive approach.
counselling: Explain that BCC is usually highly curable but continues to invade locally if ignored.
followUp: Monitor for recurrence and new keratinocyte cancers; reinforce UV protection.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient that BCC is harmless because metastasis is uncommon while the tumour continues to destroy local tissue.
oneLinePearl: BCC is usually slow, but it is still cancer and still needs definitive treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association basal cell carcinoma resources

title: Cutaneous SCC: Find the High-Risk Tumour Before It Spreads
bottomLine: Cutaneous SCC has meaningful metastatic potential. Diagnose promptly and identify high-risk features—site, size/depth, poor differentiation, recurrence, perineural symptoms and immunosuppression—because they change surgical management, nodal assessment and follow-up intensity.
recognize: SCC can present as a firm keratotic/crusted papule or plaque, nonhealing ulcer or rapidly growing tender lesion on sun-damaged skin.
differentiate: Keratoacanthoma-like lesions may behave as SCC and require diagnostic management; actinic keratosis is premalignant but can progress to SCC.
assessment: Assess growth rate, pain/numbness, diameter/location, recurrence, transplant/immunosuppression and regional nodes.
workup: Biopsy confirms diagnosis and risk features; high-risk tumours may require specialist nodal/imaging evaluation.
management: Definitive excision/Mohs or other specialist-directed treatment is based on tumour risk and anatomy; transplant/immunosuppressed patients merit lower threshold for urgent dermatology involvement.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly treat a persistent hyperkeratotic lesion with cryotherapy without biopsy when invasive SCC is plausible.
counselling: Explain that SCC differs from BCC because spread to nodes/other organs can occur, especially with high-risk features.
followUp: Ensure definitive treatment and risk-based nodal/skin surveillance.
examTrap: Treating a rapidly enlarging tender keratotic lesion as another actinic keratosis without biopsy.
oneLinePearl: SCC urgency comes from tumour biology plus host risk, not from colour alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association squamous cell carcinoma resources

title: Actinic Keratosis: Treat the Lesion and Recognize the SCC Warning Signs
bottomLine: Actinic keratoses are UV-related premalignant lesions and markers of field cancerization. Treat visible disease, choose lesion-directed versus field therapy by burden/site/patient factors, and biopsy lesions that become indurated, rapidly enlarging, tender, thick or ulcerated because invasive SCC may have developed.
recognize: Rough scaly lesions on chronically sun-exposed skin may be easier to feel than see; multiple AKs indicate substantial cumulative UV damage.
differentiate: SCC becomes more likely with induration, tenderness, rapid growth, ulceration or a persistent thick hyperkeratotic lesion.
assessment: Assess lesion number/field damage, immunosuppression, prior skin cancer and suspicious individual features.
workup: Typical thin AK is clinical; biopsy when SCC cannot be excluded.
management: Use cryotherapy for appropriate individual lesions or field therapy such as topical/photo-based approaches for broader actinic damage according to site and patient preference.
medicationSafety: Field therapies can produce expected inflammatory reactions; ensure the patient understands duration and red flags rather than stopping or overusing therapy unpredictably.
counselling: Use broad-spectrum sun protection and avoid indoor tanning; explain that treatment also creates an opportunity for future skin-cancer surveillance.
followUp: Reassess treated field and biopsy lesions that fail to resolve or evolve suspiciously.
examTrap: Repeatedly freezing a thickening painful lesion without reconsidering invasive SCC.
oneLinePearl: An AK that changes character has earned a biopsy question.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association actinic keratosis resources

title: Pigmented Lesions: Compare, Evolve, and Biopsy the Outlier
bottomLine: Pigmented-lesion evaluation uses the patient's pattern, evolution and lesion-specific morphology. ABCDE/ugly-duckling and dermoscopy support risk assessment, but a clinically suspicious lesion needs histologic diagnosis rather than serial reassurance photos indefinitely.
recognize: Asymmetry, border irregularity, multiple colours, evolution and an outlier lesion increase melanoma suspicion.
Acral and nail-unit melanoma may present differently from classic sun-exposed melanomas.
differentiate: Seborrheic keratosis, lentigo, benign nevus, pigmented BCC and subungual hemorrhage are common mimics.
assessment: Ask change over time, new symptoms/bleeding, sun exposure, family/personal melanoma history, immune status and compare with the patient's other lesions.
workup: Dermoscopy improves pattern assessment when the clinician is trained; biopsy is required when melanoma/invasive malignancy remains plausible.
management: Biopsy/referral is chosen according to melanoma suspicion, anatomic site and ability to preserve diagnostic depth; low-risk stable lesions can be observed with a clear follow-up plan.
medicationSafety: Do not camouflage an undiagnosed pigmented lesion with destructive therapy before a diagnosis is secured.
redFlags: New firm nodule within a pigmented lesion
counselling: Teach what change should trigger reassessment and that melanoma can occur in any skin tone.
followUp: Use documented comparison only when observation is clinically appropriate; ensure biopsy pathology is closed-loop.
examTrap: Assuming a dark lesion in deeply pigmented skin is benign because melanoma is less common.
oneLinePearl: The lesion that is changing or different from the others deserves the most attention.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association melanoma/ABCDE skin-check resources

title: Urticaria and Angioedema: First Decide Whether the Airway Is at Risk
bottomLine: Hives are transient wheals; angioedema is deeper swelling. The first decision is whether this is anaphylaxis/airway compromise requiring IM epinephrine, then distinguish histaminergic urticaria from bradykinin-mediated angioedema and avoid broad allergy testing for uncomplicated chronic spontaneous urticaria.
recognize: Individual urticaria lesions usually move/fade within 24 hours; persistent painful bruising lesions suggest urticarial vasculitis or another mimic.
Tongue/laryngeal swelling, wheeze, hypotension or multi-system acute reaction suggests anaphylaxis.
differentiate: ACE-inhibitor/bradykinin angioedema often occurs without hives and does not respond reliably to antihistamines/epinephrine the way histaminergic disease does; however airway protection remains the priority.
assessment: Assess airway/voice/swallowing, breathing, BP, GI symptoms, timing/exposures, medications including ACE inhibitors/NSAIDs, duration and recurrence.
workup: Acute urticaria usually needs no broad lab/allergy panel; chronic spontaneous disease gets targeted testing only when history suggests an alternate diagnosis.
management: Treat anaphylaxis with prompt IM epinephrine and emergency care; use nonsedating second-generation antihistamines as first-line chronic urticaria therapy and step up according to allergy/dermatology guidance.
Stop the culprit ACE inhibitor in suspected ACE-inhibitor angioedema and provide airway-focused emergency management when significant swelling occurs.
medicationSafety: Sedating first-generation antihistamines increase cognitive/anticholinergic/fall burden and are not preferred chronic therapy.
Do not delay epinephrine while trying antihistamines or corticosteroids in anaphylaxis.
redFlags: Recurrent angioedema without hives suggesting bradykinin pathway
counselling: Teach epinephrine use/action plan after anaphylaxis and explain that chronic spontaneous urticaria is usually not caused by one hidden food allergy.
followUp: Refer recurrent severe angioedema, suspected hereditary/bradykinin disease or uncontrolled chronic urticaria.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first while a patient with hives, wheeze and hypotension deteriorates instead of giving IM epinephrine.
oneLinePearl: Hives can wait for antihistamine; anaphylaxis cannot wait for epinephrine.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology urticaria/anaphylaxis practice principles

title: Drug Eruptions: Benign Exanthem or Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reaction?
bottomLine: A new medication rash requires severity triage before naming the morphology. Mucosal disease, skin pain, blistering/detachment, facial edema, fever, organ injury or eosinophilia raises SJS/TEN, DRESS or another severe cutaneous adverse reaction and requires immediate culprit-drug cessation plus urgent hospital/specialist care.
recognize: Simple morbilliform eruptions are common and usually lack mucosal injury, skin pain and organ dysfunction.
SJS/TEN causes painful targetoid/dusky lesions, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment; DRESS often includes fever, facial edema, widespread rash, eosinophilia and internal-organ involvement.
differentiate: Viral exanthem, urticaria, AGEP, erythema multiforme and autoimmune blistering disease can mimic drug reactions.
assessment: Build a medication/start-stop timeline including OTC/herbal drugs; assess mucosa, skin pain, blistering/body-surface involvement, fever, nodes, face edema and respiratory/hepatic/renal symptoms.
workup: CBC/differential, liver/renal tests and other organ-directed evaluation are indicated when DRESS/SCAR is possible; biopsy/dermatology consultation supports uncertain severe presentations.
management: Stop the suspected culprit(s) promptly in a serious reaction and arrange emergency/hospital/dermatology care; supportive care and disease-specific treatment are specialist-led.
For uncomplicated exanthem, reassess medication necessity and provide symptom care while documenting the reaction accurately.
medicationSafety: Never rechallenge a drug that caused SJS/TEN/DRESS without specialist-level justification; update allergy/adverse-reaction records with the actual phenotype rather than 'rash' alone.
counselling: Teach the exact culprit/severe reaction and provide documentation because future re-exposure can be dangerous.
followUp: Monitor delayed organ involvement after DRESS and ensure medication records/referrals are updated.
examTrap: Calling fever, facial edema and rising liver enzymes with a widespread drug rash a benign exanthem.
oneLinePearl: In a drug rash, mucosa, skin pain and organ injury decide urgency.
sourceBasis: Health Canada severe cutaneous adverse reaction safety communications

title: Autoimmune Blistering Disease: Tense or Flaccid Blisters Are Only the Start
bottomLine: Autoimmune blistering disorders require urgent diagnostic confirmation because extensive skin/mucosal loss can cause infection, fluid/electrolyte disturbance and airway/ocular complications. Use morphology/distribution to form the differential, then biopsy lesional/perilesional skin correctly for routine histology plus direct immunofluorescence.
recognize: Bullous pemphigoid often causes intensely pruritic tense bullae in older adults; pemphigus vulgaris often causes fragile/flaccid blisters and prominent painful mucosal erosions.
differentiate: SJS/TEN, bullous drug eruption, infection, porphyria and contact dermatitis can produce blisters but require different urgent management.
assessment: Assess mucosal/ocular/airway involvement, body-surface area, infection, hydration, medications, immune disease and ability to eat/drink.
workup: Obtain appropriate dermatology-guided biopsy: lesional skin for histology and perilesional uninvolved-appearing skin for direct immunofluorescence; serology can support specific diagnoses.
management: Urgent dermatology involvement is needed for extensive or mucosal disease; systemic/topical immunosuppressive therapy depends on diagnosis/severity and requires infection/toxicity monitoring.
medicationSafety: Before significant immunosuppression, assess infection/vaccination risks and drug-specific monitoring; do not empirically immunosuppress an undifferentiated blistering infection or SCAR.
counselling: Explain that biopsy location matters and that treatment often requires specialist longitudinal monitoring.
followUp: Track mucosal/skin healing, infection and immunosuppressant complications.
examTrap: Biopsying only the centre of an eroded blister for immunofluorescence and missing the perilesional diagnostic tissue.
oneLinePearl: Blister morphology guides the differential; perilesional immunofluorescence confirms the autoimmune pattern.
sourceBasis: Canadian dermatology autoimmune blistering disease practice principles
